APPLICANTS’ RESPONSE TO KEVIN KENNEDY’S APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO.
                               35

       On September 20, 2026, intervenor Kevin Kennedy (“Mr. Kennedy”) filed a Motion for an

Independent Technical Investigation and Forensic Audit, requesting that the presiding

Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”) from the State Office of Administrative Hearings (“SOAH”)



APPLICANTS’ RESPONSE TO KEVIN KENNEDY’S APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 35              Page 1 of 9
 order the commencement of an independent technical investigation and forensic audit of the

Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. (“ERCOT”). 1 The ALJs denied Mr. Kennedy’s Motion,2

and Mr. Kennedy subsequently appealed the order on September 23, 2026 (the “Appeal”). 3

Pursuant to 16 Tex. Admin. Code (“TAC”) § 22.123(a)(4), this response to Mr. Kennedy’s Appeal

is timely filed.

                                          I.    INTRODUCTION

        Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) and LCRA Transmission Services

Corporation (“LCRA TSC” and, together with Oncor, “Applicants”) respectfully file this response

in opposition to Kevin Kennedy’s Appeal of SOAH Order No. 35. 4 Mr. Kennedy’s Appeal should

be denied for two independent reasons.

        First, the Appeal is procedurally deficient under 16 TAC § 22.123. An appeal of an interim

order must specify the reasons why the order is “unjustified or improper.” 5 Mr. Kennedy does not

identify any legal or factual error in SOAH Order No. 35. Indeed, he repeatedly relies on SOAH’s

APPLICANTS’ RESPONSE TO KEVIN KENNEDY’S APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 35                               Page 2 of 9
 ruling in support of his request for an audit of ERCOT. 6 And he agrees with the ALJs’ conclusion

that SOAH lacks self-initiating regulatory or investigative power, acknowledging the jurisdictional

basis for the denial of his request. 7 Because Mr. Kennedy concedes the order was correctly

decided, he fails to satisfy the procedural requirement to specifically identify why the order is

“unjustified” or “improper” within the meaning of the rule. Instead, Mr. Kennedy merely co-opts

the rule for appealing interim orders to present his request directly to the Commission.

         Second, the technical premises underlying Mr. Kennedy’s Appeal are factually inaccurate.

Mr. Kennedy’s arguments rest on a fundamental misunderstanding of the differences between the

Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”) and the 2024 Regional Transmission Plan (“2024 RTP”).

These two studies were designed for different purposes, used different planning horizons, and were

developed on different timelines. The differences Mr. Kennedy identifies are the natural and

expected result of sound, and layered, planning practices—not evidence of error.

         The Commission must see through Mr. Kennedy’s transparent attempt to shift attention

away from recent Commission orders that have approved other PBRP-recommended 765-kV

transmission lines in Texas. 8 With his request for an audit, and despite stating that he “does not

allege” it, Mr. Kennedy wants the Commission to believe that ERCOT “cooked the books” with

APPLICANTS’ RESPONSE TO KEVIN KENNEDY’S APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 35                                     Page 3 of 9
 its study assumptions. 9 But Mr. Kennedy’s Appeal strains to identify irregularities where none

exist, construing routine planning decisions as evidence of a flawed process. His arguments should

be rejected and his Appeal denied.

     II.       THE APPEAL IS PROCEDURALLY DEFICIENT UNDER 16 TAC § 22.123

           Under 16 TAC § 22.123(a)(3), an appeal of an interim order must “specify the reasons why

the interim order is unjustified or improper.” This requirement is not merely a formality; it defines

the scope of appellate review. This rule requires that an appeal be premised on a legal or factual

error in the order being appealed. Mr. Kennedy’s Appeal fails to meet this threshold requirement.

           Mr. Kennedy does not claim that the ALJs misapplied the law or made incorrect factual

findings in SOAH Order No. 35. To the contrary, Mr. Kennedy expressly agrees with the ALJs’

conclusion. The ALJs determined that “SOAH ALJs do not possess self-initiating regulatory or

investigative power,” citing Tex. Gov’t Code §§ 2003.021 and 2003.049, and noting that “[u]nder

the Public Utility Regulatory Act, the Commission has complete oversight and exclusive

jurisdiction over ERCOT.” 10 Mr. Kennedy does not dispute any aspect of this holding.

           Indeed, Mr. Kennedy’s Appeal acknowledges that the ALJs correctly identified the

jurisdictional distinction between SOAH and the Commission. He states that he “does not ask the

Commission to compel SOAH to become a regulatory investigative agency” and instead asks the

Commission “to recognize the jurisdictional distinction identified by the ALJs and exercise the

Commission’s own statutory authority.” 11 This concession is fatal to his Appeal. If the ALJs

correctly applied the law—as Mr. Kennedy admits—then the interim order is neither “unjustified”

nor “improper” within the meaning of 16 TAC § 22.123(a)(3).


9
           Motion at 4.
10
           SOAH Order No. 35 at 3 (59475-6597); see Tex. Gov't Code §§ 2003.021, .049; see also Tex. Util. Code §
39.151.
11
           Appeal at 5.


APPLICANTS’ RESPONSE TO KEVIN KENNEDY’S APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 35                                 Page 4 of 9
         What Mr. Kennedy is actually attempting to do is use the appellate process not to correct

an error in an interim order but to place a new, freestanding request for Commission action before

the Commission. Mr. Kennedy’s Appeal is, in substance, an original petition asking the

Commission to exercise its independent regulatory and investigative authority over ERCOT’s

modeling practices. But this abuses the purpose of 16 TAC § 22.123. The appellate mechanism

exists to correct errors in interim orders, not to serve as a vehicle for parties to request original

Commission action that was never properly before the presiding officers in the first instance.

        Moreover, Mr. Kennedy’s request, even if it were properly before the Commission, which

it is not, requests relief outside of the scope of any recognized process for a certificate of

convenience and necessity (“CCN”) docket. Mr. Kennedy cites no previous CCN docket wherein

the Commission issued a directive to ERCOT as a result of an intervenor’s motion.

 III.    MR. KENNEDY’S TECHNICAL PREMISES ARE FACTUALLY INACCURATE

        Even if Mr. Kennedy’s Appeal were procedurally proper, which it is not, the technical

premises underlying his arguments are factually inaccurate. Mr. Kennedy filed a multitude of

speculative grievances related to ERCOT’s modeling decisions, but his core contention is that the

differences between the PBRP and the 2024 RTP demonstrate errors or inconsistencies in

ERCOT’s modeling sufficient to warrant a forensic investigation into ERCOT’s planning practices

and assumptions. 12 This contention rests on fundamental misunderstandings of the purpose, scope,

and methodology of these two studies.




12
           Appeal at 8 (“The PBRP modeling methodology warrants independent review because several identified
assumptions appear potentially inconsistent with state and federal standards, as well as fundamental engineering
principles, including data consistency, contemporaneous inputs, model validation, completeness, and controlled
sensitivity analysis.”); see also Kennedy’s Motion for Technical Investigation and Audit at 2 (Sept. 20, 2026) (Item
No. 6589) (“By what reasoning did ERCOT develop two totally different models, simultaneously, side-by-side, one
for their 2024 PBRP and another their 2024-RTP?”).


APPLICANTS’ RESPONSE TO KEVIN KENNEDY’S APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 35                                   Page 5 of 9
          The PBRP and the 2024 RTP were not intended to represent the same planning case. The

PBRP was a special-purpose regional study focused on the Permian Basin; its extra-high voltage

(“EHV”) analysis examined a 2038 planning horizon. 13 The 2024 RTP, by contrast, was a system-

wide planning assessment for the 2030 planning horizon. 14 In other words, one study examined

regional reliability considerations while the other study evaluated how those considerations fit

within the broader needs of the ERCOT electric system. The two studies served fundamentally

different purposes and, as a result, appropriately used different inputs and assumptions.

         The PBRP was developed in response to the Commission’s Order in Project No. 55718,

issued in December 2023, with the intention of completing the study by July 2024. 15 As required

by House Bill 5066 (“H.B. 5066”), the load data for West Texas was based in part on load forecast

information provided by transmission service providers (“TSPs”). 16 It also included future oil and

gas demand studied by S&P Global.17 The rest of the system load outside of West Texas was based

on the 2023 RTP load data because the 2024 RTP load data did not generally become known until

Spring 2024, and models were not finalized and distributed until December 2024, months after the

by 2030. See Applicants’ Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 31 (Sept. 2, 2026) (Item No. 6484).

APPLICANTS’ RESPONSE TO KEVIN KENNEDY’S APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 35                                       Page 6 of 9
 initial PBRP study was completed and approved by the Commission. 18 This sequencing is not

evidence of error; it reflects the practical reality of conducting a special-purpose study on ever-

changing transmission topology and a system with a large amount of load growth in a short window

of time.

        Utilizing the most recent model as the base model is the appropriate and common practice

when modeling regional studies. The regional study will then update the load and topology in the

study area (here, the Permian Basin), while retaining much of the established system-wide starting

case. Generation and dispatch are then updated and balanced in accordance with the applicable

modeling rules and study methodology.

        The fact that different studies with different assumptions demonstrate the effectiveness of

the proposed infrastructure is a feature of sound planning practice, not evidence of error. Scenario

studies intentionally vary generation and load patterns. The relevant test is whether the

recommended facilities remain needed across credible dispatch and load sensitivities—not

whether every planning case contains identical generation and load inputs.

        Additionally, Mr. Kennedy’s comparison of approximately 17,000 MW of generation in

the PBRP versus approximately 59,000 MW in the 2024 RTP is an apples-to-oranges comparison

that fundamentally mischaracterizes the two studies. 19 As stated above, the PBRP was a

regional/area-focused study. In recognized planning practices, a regional study updates the load

and topology in the study area and retains much of the existing system-wide starting case for the

remaining parts of the system outside of the study area. Generation and dispatch are then added as

APPLICANTS’ RESPONSE TO KEVIN KENNEDY’S APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 35                               Page 7 of 9
 necessary to balance the study. In the PBRP study, ERCOT added generators from the February

2024 Generator Interconnection Status (“GIS”) report with a Commercial Operations Date prior

to December 31, 2029, totaling approximately 17,170 MW across 89 generation units. 20 The 2024

RTP had a broader objective and updated load, generation, and topology across the entire ERCOT

system. It therefore contained materially more new statewide load and associated generation than

the PBRP case.

       Finally, Mr. Kennedy’s argument that the PBRP must comply with NERC Reliability

Standard TPL-001-5.1 conflates the requirements applicable to ERCOT’s annual planning

assessment (the RTP) with those applicable to special-purpose studies. 21 TPL-001-5.1 governs

ERCOT’s annual planning assessment responsibilities, which are fulfilled through the RTP

process. It does not require every special-purpose study to be a standalone annual planning

assessment using the identical case as the RTP. ERCOT performs RTP studies annually to

demonstrate compliance with NERC standards, as well as to identify improvements and propose

solutions. Special ERCOT studies like the PBRP are not required to, and generally are not intended

to, independently demonstrate compliance with NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1. They

are focused on achieving a study scope for a specific purpose. Here, the purpose is the legislative

mandate under H.B. 5066 to develop a reliability plan for the Permian Basin.

                             IV.     CONCLUSION AND PRAYER

       For the reasons stated above, including that Mr. Kennedy’s appeal is procedurally improper

and that both the 2024 RTP and the PBRP found that the projects were needed despite varying

load assumptions, Applicants respectfully request that the Commission deny Mr. Kennedy’s

Appeal of SOAH Order No. 35 in its entirety.

     II.       THE APPEAL IS PROCEDURALLY DEFICIENT UNDER 16 TAC § 22.123

           Under 16 TAC § 22.123(a)(3), an appeal of an interim order must "specify the reasons why

the interim order is unjustified or improper." This requirement is not merely a formality; it defines

the scope of appellate review. This rule requires that an appeal be premised on a legal or factual

error in the order being appealed. Mr. Kennedy' s Appeal fails to meet this threshold requirement.

           Mr. Kennedy does not claim that the ALJs misapplied the law or made incorrect factual

findings in SOAH Order No. 35. To the contrary, Mr. Kennedy expressly agrees with the ALJs'

conclusion. The ALJs determined that "SOAH ALJs do not possess self-initiating regulatory or

investigative power," citing Tex. Gov't Code §§ 2003.021 and 2003.049, and noting that "[ulnder

the Public Utility Regulatory Act, the Commission has complete oversight and exclusive

jurisdiction over ERCOT."10 Mr. Kennedy does not dispute any aspect of this holding.

           Indeed, Mr. Kennedy' s Appeal acknowledges that the ALJs correctly identified the

jurisdictional distinction between SOAH and the Commission. He states that he "does not ask the

Commission to compel SOAH to become a regulatory investigative agency" and instead asks the

Commission "to recognize the jurisdictional distinction identified by the ALJs and exercise the

Commission's own statutory authority."11 This concession is fatal to his Appeal. If the ALJs

correctly applied the law-as Mr. Kennedy admits-then the interim order is neither "unjustified"

nor "improper" within the meaning of 16 TAC § 22.123(a)(3).

       Finally, Mr. Kennedy' s argument that the PBRP must comply with NERC Reliability

Standard TPL-001-5.1 conflates the requirements applicable to ERCOT' s annual planning

assessment (the RTP) with those applicable to special-purpose studies.21 TPL-001-5.1 governs

ERCOT' s annual planning assessment responsibilities, which are fulfilled through the RTP

process. It does not require every special-purpose study to be a standalone annual planning

assessment using the identical case as the RTP. ERCOT performs RTP studies annually to

demonstrate compliance with NERC standards, as well as to identify improvements and propose

solutions. Special ERCOT studies like the PBRP are not required to, and generally are not intended

to, independently demonstrate compliance with NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1. They

are focused on achieving a study scope for a specific purpose. Here, the purpose is the legislative

mandate under H.B. 5066 to develop a reliability plan for the Permian Basin.
